brief_context: Describes fish grilling traditions along the Mediterranean shores.
brief_extract: Fennel Sauce and Gooseberry Sauce are traditional English sauces to serve with boiled or grilled mackerel. Along the Mediterranean shores, fish is often grilled over a fire of fennel stalks so that it is flavoured by the aromatic smoke. The leaves, which look like much divided fronds, are used in the sauce.

brief_context: Dill is extensively used as a garnish in Scandinavia.
brief_extract: Do not boil this sauce. Dill, a herb with a caraway flavour, is extensively used as a garnish for fish in Scandinavian countries and may also be used in sauce in the same way as fennel. Gooseberry Sauce is made in the same way as apple sauce, but the stewed fruit would have to be pulped in an electric liquidiser or sieved by hand.

brief_context: Location of the Design Centre and the safety exhibition.
brief_extract:
A. ZWEIGBERGK
Director and Secretary, British Electrical Approvals Board for Domestic Appliances
THIS was the title of an exhibition which recently attracted great public attention at the Design Centre in London, since it showed how the British Electrical Approvals Board for Domestic Appliances safeguards users against hazards in the use of appliances. “How can one be sure that an electric fire is safe and that an electric blanket will not set fire to the bed?” are two of the many questions which are voiced by the thinking members of the public, and the function of BEAB is to provide this assurance based on very stringent testing to specific standards.

brief_context: Location of appliance factories visited for safety assessments.
brief_extract: The Certificate, which is issued at the time of approval, is only renewed each year if BEAB is satisfied that no deterioration in standard has taken place. Every factory in the U.K. is visited at least once a year to assess the quality of the products under manufacture and to select samples, when considered necessary, for check testing at the Appliance Testing Laboratories of the Electricity Council, which undertake all the testing work for BEAB.

brief_context: Region where BEAB has conducted factory surveillance visits.
brief_extract: In addition, there is a system whereby information is collected and collated from outside sources on the behaviour of approved appliances, especially from Electricity Boards. A number of visits has already taken place to factories in Europe, and arrangements are in hand to obtain independent surveillance information on approved appliances which are manufactured in more distant lands. There are now upwards of 140 manufacturers in the U.K.

brief_extract:

VISIT TO BRINTON’S CARPET FACTORY, KIDDERMINSTER
by Mrs. A.

brief_context: Branch location of Mrs. A. Scullin.
article_title: VISIT TO BRINTON’S CARPET FACTORY, KIDDERMINSTER
brief_extract:
A. Scullin, Magazine Secretary, Derby

High quality Wilton and Axminster carpets are woven at the factory from a mixture of wool and a smaller percentage of nylon. Members followed the progress of the raw material through the processes of carding, ring-spinning, doubling and reeling into 1 lb.

location_standardised: Sutton Coldfield, West Midlands, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Branch location of Mrs. E. Dinenage.
brief_extract:
E. Dinenage, Magazine Secretary, Sutton Coldfield

Members visited the latest and largest newspaper offices in Europe. First they toured the basement where the sub-station is situated, housing seven transformers, supplying 8,400 kW, 12,000 kW ultimately, and Press Control Panels.

brief_context: Location of the E.A.W. Branch that visited the factory.
brief_extract:
D. Burdett, Member, Aylesbury

Return the bottles! How often have we read this on our 'Lucozade' bottles and wondered what happened to them upon their return to the factory.

brief_context: Location of the E.A.W. Branch that visited the power station.
brief_extract:
C. Nicholson, Magazine Secretary, Southport

The Southport Branch visited the Central Electricity Generating Board's 178,000 kilowatt power station at Barton, near Manchester. They were shown the twin boiler houses which contain twelve oil-fired and two coal-fired, chain grate stoker boilers, and five turbo-generators, the most powerful of which generates 50,000 kilowatts of power.

location_standardised: Barton, Greater Manchester, England, United Kingdom

location_standardised: Manchester, Greater Manchester, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Large city near which Barton power station is situated.
brief_extract:
C. Nicholson, Magazine Secretary, Southport

The Southport Branch visited the Central Electricity Generating Board's 178,000 kilowatt power station at Barton, near Manchester. They were shown the twin boiler houses which contain twelve oil-fired and two coal-fired, chain grate stoker boilers, and five turbo-generators, the most powerful of which generates 50,000 kilowatts of power.

location_standardised: Manchester Ship Canal, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Source of cooling water for Barton power station.
brief_extract: The condensers, which contain 31 miles of tubing, turn superheated steam from the turbines back into water for use once again in the boilers. When generating at full capacity Barton power station uses 10 million gallons of water each hour from the Ship Canal. A highlight of the tour was a visit to the control room from which go out instructions for the control of the station's plant and equipment.

brief_context: Venue for the International Congress of Women Engineers.
brief_extract:
Caroline Haslett Memorial Trust
The activities of the Caroline Haslett Memorial Trust also bring us into close touch with young people in this country and overseas. The Trust was particularly pleased to be able to help a number of young women engineers from the developing countries to attend the International Congress of Women Engineers and Scientists at Cambridge in July 1967. Another interesting project was the offer for the first time of a bursary for a woman designer in the Domestic Electrical Appliances Section of the International Design Competition sponsored by the Royal Society of Arts.

brief_context: Pupils from here won a prize rose-bowl.
Students here take the Home Electricity Certificate Course.
brief_extract:
Home Electricity Course
The Home Electricity Certificate Course makes
an appeal to many kinds of student, and the first
photograph shows the pupils from Elgin Aca-
demy who won the Councillor Miss Walter Rose-
bowl in 1967, having gained the highest average
marks during the year. Students from Worcester Technical College
have taken the Certificate Course as part of the
Basic Home Management Course in their first
year, since they find that a knowledge of elec-
tricity and its practical application is invaluable
for such subjects as basic cookery, housecraft
and needlework. Many of the girls will continue
their training with a further two years' study of
home economics or institutional management.

brief_context: School where pupils took the Home Electricity Course.
brief_extract:
Many of the girls will continue
their training with a further two years' study of
home economics or institutional management. Girls from the Hill School, Upton-on-Severn
who took the Home Electricity Course came
from town and country homes and their in-
terests and future careers are very varied. They
include child nursing, nursery nursing, banking,
secretarial work, physical education, reception
work, art and several girls wished to attend
technical college for courses in such subjects as
beauty and hairdressing.

Fluorescent and filament lighting sensibly combined; direct lighting from fittings with sparkling cores and smoky cover-glasses over the table, supplemented by table lamps and fluorescent tubes below the low podium on the right, behind vertical pelmets and in the suspended canopy
EAW members who visited the British Lighting Council exhibit on the Electricity Council stand at the Ideal Home Exhibition in March will have seen not only a display of interior and exterior lighting fittings, but a feature consisting of four domestic settings, each illustrating basic lighting principles. article_title: Home Economics in the Service of International Co-operation
brief_extract:
Home Economics in the Service of International
Co-operation

by MARY GEORGE, MBE, Companion IEE, Director EAW

THIS was the theme of the International Congress on Home Economics which took place at Bristol in July and was attended by one thousand delegates from some sixty countries. But what is home economics?

brief_context: Where the title 'home economics' is more familiar.
article_title: Home Economics in the Service of International Co-operation
brief_extract:
But what is home economics? It is a title not as familiar in this country as in the United States, but it is one which is now in official use. Home economics explained
The internationally recognised definition was given by Miss Frances Laidler, President of the UK Federation for Education in Home Economics, when she was speaking at our EAW Annual Luncheon in Scarborough last May.

location_standardised: Scarborough, North Yorkshire, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Location of the EAW Annual Luncheon.
article_title: Home Economics in the Service of International Co-operation
brief_extract:
It is a title not as familiar in this country as in the United States, but it is one which is now in official use. Home economics explained
The internationally recognised definition was given by Miss Frances Laidler, President of the UK Federation for Education in Home Economics, when she was speaking at our EAW Annual Luncheon in Scarborough last May. 'Home Economics today', she said, 'is the study of the family, the home and the community, in-cluding food, clothing, shelter, human relation-ships, which is very different from the old under-standing concerned as it was with the skills of cookery, laundrywork and housewifery'.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding central heating and metric measurement changes.
brief_extract:
There is the Scandinavian idea of making greater use of bedrooms, not reserving them solely for sleeping. The growing public appreciation in Britain that warmth should permeate the whole house has led to developments in the central heating field and to a greater interest in double glazing. Choice of materials
The wide choice that is now available to the householder in home planning and decoration is made possible by the growing range of new materials for structural purposes, for interior decoration of walls and surfaces and for equipment and furnishings.

brief_context: Referenced in relation to metric measurement standards.
brief_extract: Too often there is what appears to be an adequate amount of floor space but the positioning of doors and windows nullifies the value of much of it. As with the overall building of the house, standardisation and the mass production of units make for economy and speed, and the forthcoming change to metric measurements will keep Britain in line with Continental practice. Without good wiring and good lighting no home can provide real comfort and safety, and there is much to be learnt on both these subjects.

brief_context: Mentioned as having successfully transitioned to decimal currency.
article_title: It's easy when you know how
brief_extract:
For many purposes £sd will remain in use during this period, and pennies, threepenny bits and sixpences will not disappear immediately. The experience of Australia and New Zealand has shown that people quickly 'get the hang' of the new decimal currency and in these countries the period of changeover was not as long as had at first been thought necessary. Plenty of help
The Decimal Currency Board has the task of preparing the country for the changeover, and there will be an intensive publicity campaign to prepare people, using television, radio, newspaper advertising and posters, as well as material for households and schools.

brief_extract:
“For nothing worthy proving can be proven
Nor yet disproven”
Tennyson

EARLY this year the President of the Women’s Engineering Society, Dr. Betty Laverick, asked me if I would take part in a debate on the pros and cons of automation during the Society’s Annual Conference at the University of Warwick in September. As September was then some six months ahead I agreed willingly, and when asked on which side I would prefer to speak I said (thinking again that six months was a long way ahead): ‘on whichever side will help you.’ I regretted my co-operation when, about a month before the event, I received a reminding letter and a programme in which I saw that I was down to propose the motion that ‘in the opinion of the house automation is more a liability than an asset’, and that the chief speaker against this motion was no less a person than the President of the Institution of Measurement and Control.

brief_context: Location of a recent Congress on Computer Technology.
brief_extract:
Those who deal in the hardware and software of cybernetic systems have evolved their own in-language so that it is well-nigh impossible to understand what they are talking about. I first sought a simple definition of automation in one of the newest text books on the subject and all I could gather after skimming through pages of incomprehensible verbiage was that it was something to do with ‘closing the feedback loop.’ As this did not mean much to my lay mind I sought further light by looking at the titles of some of the papers presented at a recent Congress on Computer Technology in Edinburgh. I gave up when I came to the following title: ‘Partial isomorphisms in graphs and structural similarities in tree-like organic modules.’

I tried to imagine how a committee of worthy local councillors faced with the problem of whether or not to install a computer to deal with their rates assessments would cope with a keen salesman speaking this kind of language.

brief_extract: War-paint, in the case of our own primitive ancestors the indigo blue of woad, was considered an important part of a warrior's battle preparations, even although the effect might, in the main, have been psychological only. Such uses of simple pigments were widespread from earliest times, for there is evidence of all or some of them being used in North and South America, Africa, India, the Far East and in Europe. But pigments are not soluble in water and cannot therefore be used to colour fabrics and the art of dyeing developed considerably later in history.

brief_context: Origin of the cactus used to produce cochineal dye.
brief_extract: The oldest dye recorded in Western literature, and one that was known of in the time of Moses, was Kermes, which was a scarlet colour obtained from a species of scale insect. Somewhat later, cochineal was obtained also from a scale insect, one which fed on a certain Mexican cactus. Other dyes were obtained less aesthetically; for instance Indian Yellow (or Piuri) was extracted from the urine of cows that had been fed on mango leaves.

brief_context: Associated with Emperors who wore exclusive Tyrian Purple togas.
brief_extract: Other dyes were obtained less aesthetically; for instance Indian Yellow (or Piuri) was extracted from the urine of cows that had been fed on mango leaves. The rarest and most expensive dye of all, Tyrian Purple, was, at one time, reserved exclusively for colouring the royal togas of the Emperors of Rome and its use was forbidden to anyone else on pain of very unpleasant penalties. To be born 'into the purple', therefore, was a phrase of some exact significance although the actual colour itself was an arbitrary matter depending, as so many important discoveries do, on commerce.

brief_context: Where the Worshipful Company of Dyers exercised its art.
brief_extract:
Henry IV granted the first
Charter of Incorporation to the Worshipful
Company of Dyers and this was renewed by
Edward IV in 1472. By this Charter only a
Freeman of the Company could exercise the art
of dyeing in London ‘or within ten miles thereof’
and the Company kept a jealous watch on the
materials used in dyeing, imposing strict penalties
where substitutes were found to have been used. The art of dyeing with natural colouring
developed steadily but unspectacularly until the
middle of the 19th century when a young chemist,
William Perkin, accidentally discovered the first
synthetic dye and thus revolutionised the whole
industry.

brief_extract:
E. BAIRD, Magazine Secretary, Caernarvon

Caernarvon Branch members on a visit to Wylfa were able to admire examples of one of the oldest crafts of Wales and the newest technological advance in Wales. brief_context: The country where the electrical color coding changes apply.
brief_extract:
Different countries now have one or more sets
of colours. For the United Kingdom the changes will be:
RED for the LIVE wire becomes BROWN
BLACK for the NEUTRAL wire becomes BLUE
GREEN for the EARTH wire becomes STRIPED GREEN/YELLOW

FACTS ABOUT FUSES

In a 13 amp fuse there is now a choice of just two fuses:
3 amp fuse (blue) for appliances with a loading below 750 watts
13 amp fuse (brown) for appliances with a loading above 750 watts

brief_extract:
Different countries now have one or more sets
of colours. For the United Kingdom the changes will be:
RED for the LIVE wire becomes BROWN
BLACK for the NEUTRAL wire becomes BLUE
GREEN for the EARTH wire becomes STRIPED GREEN/YELLOW

FACTS ABOUT FUSES

In a 13 amp fuse there is now a choice of just two fuses:
3 amp fuse (blue) for appliances with a loading below 750 watts
13 amp fuse (brown) for appliances with a loading above 750 watts
